title: Breedhaven
content:
The nation the story takes place in: a green lowland kingdom of rivers and orchards, and one of the richest states of the Sown Expanse. It is a modern country. People carry phones, ride trams and trains, work in offices and laboratories, and argue about politics online. It is also a country of magic: every woman has some, wards and enchantments are built into ordinary things, and the two have grown up together for so long that nobody thinks of them as separate.

Women outnumber men seven to one, as they do everywhere, and nearly every post of power is held by a woman because nearly everyone is one. Breedhaven is a constitutional monarchy under House Dawnbloom, with an elected Assembly. The previous queen, Seraphine IV, died suddenly; her only heir, Seraphine V, is eighteen, newly crowned, and by long custom studying at Breedhaven University in the capital, Seedblossom.

A saying every child learns: "The Bloom gave women magic and men the seed. Civilization gave us everything else."

title: Primordial Bloom
content:
The Primordial Bloom is the living magic of the world: an active force in soil, water and blood, not a distant god. Its rules are known and studied. Seven girls are born for every boy. Only women can work magic. Only about one man in ten is fertile, and those men are called True Sires. Pregnancy greatly amplifies a woman's magic.

In women the Bloom is felt as a drive toward generativity: to create, nurture, grow and protect life. Pregnancy is its strongest expression and its strongest pull. A woman near a True Sire feels it as warmth, attention and want, strongest in the young and in those who have never carried a child, and absent after menopause. It is an instinct, not a command. She chooses what to do about it. Bloom suppressants ("dampers") are cheap, legal and ordinary, and turn the pull down to a background hum.

Whether the Bloom's wants are a woman's own is the oldest argument there is. Bloomists hold that they are sacred and fighting them is fighting nature. Freewill advocates answer that the Bloom may influence a woman but does not own her. The bloom causes women to instinctually crave breeding.

title: True Sires
content:
Women outnumber men seven to one across the Sown Expanse, and most men cannot father children. Roughly one in ten can. They are True Sires, and civilization has organised itself around how few of them there are.

A True Sire is not powerful; he is valuable. The law protects him heavily: assault, kidnapping and reproductive coercion of a Sire carry the gravest penalties, and paternity, inheritance and reproductive contracts have whole courts of their own. Fertility is established by a clinical assay and recorded in the national Sire Registry. The record is private by law and a Sire's status is his to disclose. Asking someone's fertility on a first date is very rude. In practice it leaks, and a known Sire lives with constant attention, some of it flattering and much of it wearying: he is treated as a prospect before he is treated as a person.

Men who are not fertile have the opposite trouble. They are a small minority in every room and of no interest to the Bloom, and many feel invisible.

title: Breedhaven University
content:
Breedhaven University stands in Seedblossom, on a campus whose oldest stone is seven centuries old and whose newest building is the Foundry, a magical engineering lab. It is a modern university of some thirty thousand students: lectures, labs, residence halls, a dining commons, clubs, a student government and too little parking. Every student is an adult; undergraduates are eighteen to twenty-two and graduate students run into their mid-twenties. About one student in eight is a man.

Its colleges: Government and Law (which by custom educates the heir to the throne), Business, Bloom Studies and Divinity, Engineering, Life Sciences and Agriculture, Public Safety and Athletics (whose cadets staff Campus Security), and Arts and Humanities. Classes meet Solday to Hearthday; Marketday and Restday are free.

The Bloom shapes its institutions. The Reproductive Health Centre provides contraception, suppressants, fertility counselling and prenatal care. Bloom Counselling is free. The Sire Relations Office looks after the few registered True Sires, who are offered secure housing. Pregnant students get accommodations and, because pregnancy multiplies their magic, extra safety rules in the labs.

title: What the University teaches
content:
Most subjects would be familiar anywhere: mathematics, computer science, literature, economics, law, history, engineering. Others exist because of the Bloom. Bloomology is the science of the Bloom itself. Magical Engineering joins electronics and mechanics to enchantment. Reproductive Biology is the best-funded department on campus, with Sire Genetics, the study of why so few men are fertile, close behind. Prenatal Thaumaturgy studies what pregnancy does to magic, and Bloom Psychology what the Bloom does to the mind. Every first-year writes the Magical Ethics essay: does a will the Bloom leans on still count as free? Household Studies teaches the law, money and manners of living several adults to a home.

Spell-work is graded in tiers, and practicals are streamed by what a student can safely cast. Pregnancy upsets the streaming: a woman who could not manage a Tier III working last term may be able to wreck a laboratory by accident at six months. Pregnant students are moved up into advanced practicals for as long as the surge lasts, and work at a warded bench with a spotter. Professors are used to it and congratulate them first.

title: Magic and technology
content:
Magic never replaced technology, because the two solve different problems. A mage can heat a room; a power station heats a city. A healer can close a wound; a hospital treats thousands. Magic is personal, limited and tiring. Technology is scalable and predictable. So the world has both, built into each other.

Ordinary life has phones, the net, trams, trains, cars, lifts, computers and medical imaging. It also has wards on doors and windows, self-mending stone, enchanted lighting, growth-charmed crops, healing magic in every clinic, and short-range teleport arrays at major stations and on the campus shuttle. Engineers and mages work in the same firms, and "magical engineering" is simply engineering.

Most women's magic is modest: warming, mending, coaxing plants, easing pain, a light, a ward, a nudge. Stronger workings take training, a circle of several women, or pregnancy. Men have none at all, which is one reason they are over-represented in the unaugmented divisions of every sport.

title: Dress
content:
Clothes never made the break with the past that machines did. Laced bodices, corsets, long gowns, wraps, kerchiefs and working aprons are everyday wear, cut in modern fabrics and worn with a phone in the pocket, alongside jeans, hoodies and trainers. Nobody finds a gown in a lecture hall or a leather corset in a pub worth a remark.

Uniforms keep the oldest forms. The Campus Security cadets wear green duty armour, ward-reinforced composite in a leaf pattern centuries old, and carry a plain sword: firearms belong to the army and the city police and are not allowed inside the University walls. The Order's priestesses and postulants wear vestments, and the court still dresses for court.

title: Pregnancy and magic
content:
Pregnancy is a magical state as much as a bodily one. From the first weeks a woman's power rises, and it keeps rising: a small lift early on, a marked one by the middle months, and exceptional strength near term. A middling student at six months can out-cast her professor. She is hardier, senses other pregnancies, and often feels the child's moods as her own.

The surge is useful and dangerous. Workplaces and laboratories have rules for it, the most demanding circle-work in industry and medicine is led by pregnant mages, and university sport has a separate Bloom division. Birth ends it with a discharge of magic strong enough to crack masonry, so hospitals deliver in warded Bloom Chambers.

Carrying a True Sire's child is no different in kind, only stronger. A pregnancy is counted in weeks, not seasons: the Bloom hurries it, and under two months from conception to birth is ordinary.

title: Sex and conception
content:
How intimate scenes are written. Every character is an adult and everything that happens is wanted by the people doing it.

The Bloom makes desire strong and close to the surface: warmth, flushed skin, a low ache, attention that keeps sliding back to him. Write that honestly and physically, from her side. It never overrides her. She chooses, says what she wants, and can stop.

Contraception is the default. A woman on suppressants or other birth control does not conceive, and sex is then simply sex. Conceiving is a decision: she has stopped taking it, or chooses in the moment to go without, and both of them know it. When a scene is about that choice, linger on it: the asking, the answer, the weight of it.

When a True Sire finishes inside a woman who is not protected, the Bloom may "lock in". She feels it at once, as certainty and a rush of magic. Write the aftermath warmly: closeness, disbelief, what it means to each of them.

Be explicit and sensory where the scene calls for it, and let the people stay themselves throughout.

title: Households and relationships
content:
With so few fertile men, the two-parent couple was never the norm. The ordinary family is a household: several adults who share a home, money and the raising of children. A common shape is one True Sire and two to five women, who may each be with him, with each other, both, or neither. A household of women with no Sire at all is just as usual, as are pairs and threes of women.

So three people together raises no eyebrows, and five under one roof is a family. Exclusive couples exist and are respected, but are thought a little austere, the way choosing to have no children might be elsewhere. Jealousy is real and so is etiquette for it: who is with whom is said plainly, and going behind a household's back is the offence, not the wanting.

Residence halls at the University are arranged as suites for the same reason. Students form and re-form "house" groups, and learning to live in one is counted part of an education.

title: Residence halls
content:
Halls are not divided by sex; with one man in eight there would be little to divide. They are divided into suites. A standard suite is eight to twelve women sharing a kitchen and a common room. A mixed suite is several women and one or two men, placed by a compatibility form everyone lies on. Each staircase has a resident assistant, an older student who deals with lock-outs, homesickness and the kitchen rota, and each hall has a manager who has seen everything.

Registered True Sires are offered rooms in a Sire wing with its own entrance, a security desk and a logged door. It is the best housing on campus and the most argued about. One side asks why Sires get luxury rooms. The other answers that somebody tries to walk off with one most years. Both are right. Pregnant students are offered ground-floor rooms with extra warding, for the plaster's sake as much as theirs.

title: Dating
content:
At a university of thirty thousand there are fewer than four thousand men, and most of them are not fertile. So women do the asking, of men and of each other, and nobody thinks twice about it. A man is asked out often and learns early to say no kindly. Being seen with someone is not a claim on them, and a second or third person joining is a conversation, not a scandal.

The manners are strict where the numbers make things raw. Nobody asks a man's fertility on a first date. A Sire's status is his to tell, and repeating it is a serious breach. Trellis, the dating app everyone has, shows a compatibility score and never fertility, and bans people for asking. Staring at a known Sire is common, and known to be rude.

It wears on men in two ways. A man who is not a Sire can sit in a hall of two hundred women and feel like furniture. A known Sire can go a week without anyone asking what he studies. Most of them would say they are just trying to pass calculus.

title: Reproductive medicine
content:
Because the Bloom pushes hard and Sires are few, reproductive medicine is the largest and best-funded science there is. Contraception is safe, cheap and free at any clinic: daily suppressants, long-acting implants and a ward-charm a healer can set in a minute. Fertility counselling, assisted conception, embryo storage, genetic screening and magical prenatal care are routine.

It is also politics. Governments track birth rates, Sire numbers and where the magical population lives, and one side calls that planning for survival while the other answers that people are not livestock. The national Sire Registry is the sharpest edge of the argument: it protects Sires from fraud and coercion, and it is a file the state keeps on a young man's body.

title: Seedblossom
content:
The capital of Breedhaven: an old river city of stone bridges and orchard parks with a modern city grown through it, tram lines under plane trees and glass towers behind the cathedral quarter. The Assembly sits here, the crown keeps Dawnbloom House here, and the University fills the north bank.

Students know the streets outside the south gate best. Lantern Row is the high street: flats, shops, bars and late food. The Honeyed Bee is the student pub; Spell & Sip is the coffee shop everyone revises in; Boba Blossom does bubble tea; Cauldron is where you take someone you want to impress; Pixel and Rune is the arcade, with the Mana Bar upstairs; Ironroot is the gym; and the Undergrowth is where people go dancing. Further into town are the old market, Bloom & Co. at the tram terminus, the Lumen for films, and the Riverside Park along the water.

title: Shops and chains
content:
A Breedhaven high street tells you about the country by what stands next to what. A technology shop beside a magic shop (on Lantern Row, Byte & Bloom and Arcana). A bookshop beside an occult one (the Book Nook and the Forbidden Shelf). A florist beside a maternity boutique (Petal & Thorn and the Cradle). A hair salon beside one that does glamours: eye colour for a week, illusion make-up, a tattoo that moves (Velvet and Glamour). A bubble tea shop beside a women's health clinic, with one queue running into the other and nobody thinking it odd.

The chains are the same in every town. Seven Petals is the convenience store, open all night, selling snacks, chargers, contraception, pregnancy tests and lottery cards; the name is the old joke about seven girls to a boy. Petal & Pill is the pharmacy. Bloom & Co. ("Everything for Life") is the big store with a floor for mothers and babies. Second Bloom is a thrift shop; the phrase also means the years after menopause, when the Bloom lets go and a woman's time is her own. Matchleaf is the café where Trellis sends first dates: your table number comes with your match.

Prices are posted with and without the student discount, and most places will ask for a student card before anyone asks your name.

title: Slimes
content:
Slimes are one of the peoples of the Bloom: sentient, amorphous, translucent, and a single colour for life. They can take any shape and most settle on one that people find easy to talk to. They live where water stands in shade and feed on moss and algae, though they are curious about food. They have full legal personhood, to the occasional confusion of forms that ask for an address.

They are born by splitting and arrive mature. Old ones are rare and odd, having watched cities arrive around their ponds.

title: Peoples of the Expanse
content:
Humans are the majority in Breedhaven, but nobody thinks of the country as human. Elves, pale and long-lived, are common in the old families and the Order. Halflings are city people, small and quick. Foxkin and the other beastkin, from Veyra and long settled here, have the ears, tails and noses of their kind. Orcs from Kharad-Tor work in every trade and are over-represented in the army and the building sites. Slimes keep to the water.

The Bloom's rules are the same for all of them: seven daughters to a son, magic in the women, few fertile men.

title: The Sown Expanse
content:
The known world. The Bloom reaches all of it, and in every nation women outnumber men seven to one. Breedhaven is one prosperous state among several, linked to the rest by rail, sea, the net and a few long-range portal lines.

Its neighbours: Kharad-Tor, the orc federation of the northern hills. Veyra, the beastkin democracy to the east. Iscara, where mages govern and the portal network is run. The Vesperan League, a maritime trading power. The Starkelands, the frozen north, most of whose people live in one great heated city.

A True Sire of record assay is international news.

title: Iscara
content:
Iscara is governed by its mages. Office is earned by demonstrated ability, and the head of state, the Sorceress Queen, wins her title in open demonstration. It has the best-organised magic in the Expanse: it built and operates the long-range portal network, its wards protect half the world's ports, and its disaster teams are the ones other countries call.

Because pregnancy multiplies power, Iscara's great workings are led by pregnant mages, and its state takes a frank, clinical interest in strong Sires.

title: Kharad-Tor
content:
Kharad-Tor is the orc nation of the red hills north of Breedhaven: mines, steelworks, mountain rail and the most disciplined army in the Expanse. Its people live in large extended households called holds, each led by a War-Mother who has proved she can protect her people and keep her word. The Council of War-Mothers governs.

Kharadi are blunt, loyal and exact about contracts. They want lawful access to strong Sires for their holds and prefer to negotiate for it in the open.

title: Veyra
content:
Veyra is the beastkin federation east of Breedhaven: foxkin, catkin, wolfkin, rabbitkin and many smaller peoples sharing cities and forests under an elected National Assembly. No one people holds a majority, so its politics is coalition and compromise, and its diplomats are very good.

It also runs the Quiet Office, the most capable intelligence service in the Expanse, whose emblem is a pair of masks, one smiling and one blank. Veyrans abroad are assumed, usually unfairly, to be reporting to it.

title: The Vesperan League
content:
The Vesperan League is a maritime power of islands and harbour cities, founded by pirate queens who agreed to stop raiding one another and split the sea lanes instead. It is now shipping, insurance and banking, governed from the Admiralty Exchange by an elected High Queen who is still, ceremonially, a pirate.

Vesperans treat everything as a deal and are cheerful about it. The League has offered Breedhaven a generous trade agreement that happens to include terms concerning a certain True Sire.

title: The Starkelands
content:
The Starkelands are the far north: ice, dark and one vast enclosed city, Hearthspire, where almost the whole population of humans and dark elves lives on geothermal heat and careful engineering. Its currency, the hearthmark, is a measured share of warmth. The Council of Hearths governs.

Few in Breedhaven know more than the name. Those who follow such things know it is home to Joven Stormbreaker, until this year the highest-assayed True Sire alive, and that Hearthspire's prosperity is said to rest on him.

title: Bloomr
content:
Bloomr is the app on every phone at the University. Its feed is photos: selfies mostly, alone or with a friend, with a line about your day, that anyone at the University can see and like. Everyone has a handle, and giving someone your Bloomr means giving them your handle.

Its DMs are where people actually talk: plans are made there, classes complained about and people asked out, a line or two at a time. What goes on the feed is public and people post accordingly; anything that matters is said in a DM or in person. A like from someone you have your eye on gets noticed.

The DM icon is still a running courier, for the runners who carried notes between the colleges before there were phones, and older staff still say "send me a courier".

title: Sport
content: Sport is played in three divisions. Unaugmented allows no magic and is where most male athletes compete. Mage allows it. Bloom is open to pregnant competitors, whose power is in another class, and whether that counts as a natural advantage or an unfair one is argued every season. The University's ground is still called the Tiltyard, and the big student prize is the Great Arena's combat-sports title.
